messages.subject: non-invasive marking of points?
parts:
Hi All,

We are working in a national park with a =93non-invasive research=94 policy =
in
effect. This means we cannot mark point count stations with any obvious
signs such as flagging, tree tags, or paint. An acceptable method to
permanently mark a point is to place a nail in a wooden stake and drive
this in so that it is flush with the ground and then use a metal detector
to relocate this point. Well, I=92m about to drive a stake into myself! We=

have over 200 points in this study and it just doesn=92t seem reasonable to
carry a metal detector in the field. We want these points to be permanent
since this will be part of a long term monitoring study which will include
vegetation sampling.

First, does anyone have experience with or suggestions for non-invasively
marking points? Second is it necessary to sample the exact location every
time? We will be using a GPS unit to mark and relocate points which under
average conditions gets us to within 10-20 m of the point.

Thanks so much and happy field days to you all!
Kim Ferree

messages.author: 082ede990d64de46
messages.subject: Re: non-invasive marking of points?
parts:
Hi Kimberley

I have a system which I use for discreet marking of points where the
situation requires. I use a tree which is in the vicinity and is clearly
identifiable- take a photo & write a description & use your GPS to find it
the next time. Then I use a magnetic bearing and measured distance from the
tree to the point location.

When you need to go back to the point it is just a matter of standing out
from the tree and finding the point at the distance and bearing from the
tree. I have no trouble finding a small peg even in thick ground cover this
way and I use this method for relocating individual plants being monitored
often over years.

I use a Leica Disto Classic 3 and a Suunto KB14/360 R. This will certainly
get you standing in the same spot each time.

Cheers

Colin Driscoll

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: non-invasive marking of points?
parts:
I agree with Colin that relocation isn't too problematic provided you have
good notes. Laser rangefinders make it easy to record exact distances to
help locate points. Having a photo of a useful feature near the point
seems an excellent idea. Apart from the issue of carrying a metal
detector around, you would need to achieve much better accuracy than
10-20m, to be able to find the peg in a reasonable time, so a written
description of the location would be needed anyway.

Accuracy in relocating the point is less important for bird surveys than
for plant surveys, and for most purposes, the nearest 10-20m may be OK.
But a brief written description should allow you to improve this accuracy
appreciably, even if you didn't bother to relocate the point exactly.

Steve Buckland
